notice: RN bank batch 120: Renal case studies: missed hemodialysis, PD peritonitis, triple-whammy AKI and an infected kidney stone. Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md. Also carries the bank-wide catalog (catalog.py): the RN Question Bank and every curated test set.

subtopics.name: Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate action.

cells: Peaked T, wide QRS, flat P

rationale.correct: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes and pulmonary edema after missed dialysis is an emergency.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Place the hyperkalemia treatments in order of how quickly they act on the heart and the serum potassium, from fastest to slowest.

items.text: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate: binds potassium in the gut over hours
IV regular insulin with dextrose: shifts potassium into cells within 15 to 30 minutes
IV calcium gluconate: stabilizes the heart muscle within minutes
Nebulized albuterol: also shifts potassium into cells
Hemodialysis: removes potassium from the body

rationale.correct: Calcium protects the heart first, insulin and albuterol shift potassium, binders and dialysis remove it.

perOption.a: Protects the heart but does not lower potassium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: The most immediate threat is {{b1}}; the next is {{b2}}; both are fixed definitively by {{b3}}.

rationale.correct: Hyperkalemia threatens the heart first; urgent dialysis removes potassium and fluid.

perOption.b1:a: Wide QRS can progress to a sine wave and arrest.
perOption.b1:b: Possible, but not the most immediate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The protocol orders regular insulin 0.1 units/kg (maximum 10 units) IV with 25 g of dextrose. The client weighs 84 kg. How many units of insulin should the nurse prepare? Round to the nearest whole unit.

rationale.correct: 0.1 x 84 = 8.4 units, rounded to 8 units per the protocol; below the 10-unit maximum. Many protocols now use 5 units in kidney failure to reduce hypoglycemia, and glucose is checked hourly for 4 to 6 hours.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

exhibits.title: Hyperkalemia protocol
exhibits.body: Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV over 10 minutes. Regular insulin 0.1 units/kg IV (round to the nearest whole unit, maximum 10) with dextrose 50% 50 mL. Albuterol 10 mg nebulized. Emergency hemodialysis. Weight 84 kg.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take while dialysis is arranged? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give calcium gluconate IV on a cardiac monitor
Check glucose every hour after the insulin
Raise the head of the bed and give oxygen
Avoid blood pressure checks and IV lines in the fistula arm
Give the client a banana for the hypoglycemia risk

rationale.correct: Stabilize the heart, watch glucose after insulin, treat the edema and protect the fistula.

perOption.b: Hypoglycemia is common, especially in kidney failure.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: After dialysis, review the findings. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Potassium 4.6 mEq/L; ECG normal
Weight 79.5 kg; lungs clear
Glucose 58 mg/dL 3 hours after insulin
No reliable transport to dialysis
Thrill and bruit present over the fistula

rationale.correct: Potassium and fluid are corrected; hypoglycemia and the transport barrier need action.

perOption.r4:c1: A case manager or social worker must arrange transport to prevent a repeat.
perOption.r4:c2: A case manager or social worker must arrange transport to prevent a repeat.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate what it shows.

rows.text: Effluent white cells 640 with 70% neutrophils
Gram-positive cocci
Draining less than instilled for 2 days
Raised blood pressure
Some glucose absorption from the dialysate

rationale.correct: Peritonitis inflames the membrane, so ultrafiltration falls and fluid is retained.

perOption.r2:c1: Often skin organisms from touch contamination.
perOption.r2:c2: Often skin organisms from touch contamination.
perOption.r2:c3: Often skin organisms from touch contamination.

options.text: Heparin in the dialysate for fibrin

rationale.correct: Intraperitoneal antibiotics, heparin for fibrin, follow-up counts and exit-site care.

perOption.f: Usually only for failed treatment or certain organisms.

exhibits.title: Orders
exhibits.body: Vancomycin and ceftazidime intraperitoneally. Heparin 500 units/L in bags. Retrain technique.

questions.stem: The nurse retrains the client on a manual exchange. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Connect the new bag using aseptic technique without touching the connectors
Drain the used fluid, then fill with the new solution
Close windows, remove pets and clean the work surface
Put on a mask and perform hand hygiene
Inspect the drained fluid and record the volume
Check the bag: concentration, expiry, clarity and leaks

rationale.correct: Clean environment, mask and hands, check the bag, aseptic connection, drain then fill, inspect.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of acute kidney injury.

questions.stem: For each factor, indicate how it reduced kidney perfusion. Each row may have more than one answer.

rows.text: Hydrochlorothiazide
Diarrhea
Ibuprofen
Lisinopril

rationale.correct: Volume loss, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors together (the triple whammy) collapse filtration pressure.

perOption.r4:c1: Blocks angiotensin II, which normally keeps filtration pressure up.
perOption.r4:c2: Blocks angiotensin II, which normally keeps filtration pressure up.
perOption.r4:c3: Blocks angiotensin II, which normally keeps filtration pressure up.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

content.template: This is {{b1}} acute kidney injury; if perfusion is not restored, it may progress to {{b2}}.

rationale.correct: Prerenal AKI can become intrinsic ATN if perfusion stays low.

perOption.b1:a: Low urine sodium and a clear cause of low perfusion.

questions.stem: For each order, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: Hold lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and ibuprofen
IV isotonic fluid bolus, then reassess
Strict intake and output with daily weights
Ketorolac for the knee pain
Potassium chloride in the IV fluid
Acetaminophen for knee pain within daily limits

rationale.correct: Stop the culprits, restore volume, monitor closely and use safer analgesia.

exhibits.title: Orders
exhibits.body: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L, then 100 mL/hour. Hold home antihypertensives and NSAIDs.

questions.stem: On day 4, urine output rises sharply. Review the findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Replace fluid losses as prescribed and monitor weight
Watch for orthostatic hypotension and falls
Restart lisinopril now that urine output is high
Restrict fluids to 1 L a day

rationale.correct: The recovery (diuretic) phase of AKI needs fluid and electrolyte replacement.

perOption.a: The diuretic phase can cause dehydration.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Take action in the diuretic phase of AKI.

questions.stem: Before discharge, for each item, indicate whether it is safe or needs correction.

rows.text: Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL
Discharge list still includes ibuprofen as needed
Client told to stop lisinopril and diuretic if vomiting or diarrhea (sick-day rules)
Lisinopril restarted at a lower dose with a creatinine check in 1 week
No one told the client's pharmacy about the NSAID problem

rationale.correct: Kidney function recovered; the medication list and pharmacy need correcting.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of an obstructed infected kidney.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it is accurate or inaccurate.

rows.text: Antibiotics alone will not clear infection behind an obstruction
A 7 mm stone may pass on its own once infection is treated
Raised creatinine can be from obstruction (postrenal) plus sepsis
Straining all urine helps identify the stone type
The client should restrict fluids to reduce pain

rationale.correct: Infected obstruction needs decompression as well as antibiotics.

perOption.r2:c1: Stones over 5 to 6 mm often need intervention.
perOption.r2:c2: Stones over 5 to 6 mm often need intervention.
perOption.r5:c1: Fluids are not restricted; the focus is drainage.
perOption.r5:c2: Fluids are not restricted; the focus is drainage.

questions.stem: A right nephrostomy tube was placed. Six hours later, review the findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the tube and drainage bag for kinks or clots
Report the stopped drainage and new flank pain
Flush the tube with a large volume of saline on your own
Pull the tube back a little to free it

rationale.correct: A nephrostomy that stops draining is checked for kinks and reported.

perOption.d: Only gentle, small flushes if prescribed.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action for a nephrostomy problem.

questions.stem: The stone was calcium oxalate. Before discharge, for each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll drink enough to pass 2.5 liters of urine a day."
"I'll cut out all calcium foods."
"I'll eat less salt and fewer high-oxalate foods like spinach."
"I'll strain my urine and bring any stone in."
"I'll take vitamin C 2 grams daily for my immune system."

rationale.correct: Fluids, normal calcium, less salt and oxalate, and avoiding high-dose vitamin C prevent stones.

perOption.r2:c1: Low calcium raises oxalate absorption; normal dietary calcium is advised.
perOption.r2:c2: Low calcium raises oxalate absorption; normal dietary calcium is advised.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

exhibits.body: Stone removed by ureteroscopy after the infection cleared.

caseStudies.title: Missed hemodialysis with hyperkalemia and fluid overload

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0700
exhibits.body: A 58-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis Monday, Wednesday and Friday missed Friday and Monday sessions because of transport problems. The client reports weakness, numb hands and shortness of breath lying down. Crackles to mid-lung fields, 3+ ankle edema, jugular veins distended. Left forearm arteriovenous fistula. Weight 84 kg (dry weight 79 kg).

rows.label: ECG
cells: Peaked T waves, wide QRS 0.14 s, flattened P waves

exhibits.title: Home dialysis clinic
exhibits.body: A 49-year-old client does continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (four exchanges a day). Since yesterday the client has had abdominal pain and the drained fluid looks cloudy. The client admits doing exchanges in the kitchen with the window open and the dog nearby, and sometimes skipping the mask. The exit site is red with crusting.

rows.label: Drain volume
cells: Less than the volume instilled for 2 days

caseStudies.title: Acute kidney injury from an NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic

exhibits.title: Medical unit
exhibits.body: A 76-year-old client with hypertension takes lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. For a week the client took ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for knee pain and had diarrhea for 3 days. The client is dizzy and has passed little urine.

caseStudies.title: Infected obstructing kidney stone with urosepsis

exhibits.title: Emergency department
exhibits.body: A 45-year-old client has severe, colicky right flank pain spreading to the groin, nausea, and blood in the urine. Since this morning the client has had shaking chills. CT: a 7 mm stone in the right ureter with hydronephrosis.

rows.label: Urinalysis
cells: Nitrites, many white cells and bacteria

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
